entries.clue: Morph: OK, OK Mr Hart, here we have an artist (4,6)

indicatorNotes.Morph: to morph is to change shape, so the letters take a new form

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: A roll-call from old children's art television: Morph the plasticine figure and his presenter.
annotation.walkthrough: Morph was a plasticine character on Tony Hart's British children's art programmes, so the surface points at one artist while the letters make another, the American painter of colour-field canvases.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Latvian-born American painted the huge blurred colour blocks of Abstract Expressionism.

entries.clue: Everyman, having taken on work, to look miserable (4)

indicatorNotes.having taken on: to take on staff is to bring them in, so ME brings OP inside itself

blocks.note: the setter refers to himself, so Everyman = ME
op = opus, a work

annotation.surface: The setter complains that taking on another job has left him glum.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter's pseudonym in a clue usually stands for ME or I; here M(OP)E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb means to wander about listless and gloomy, which is how one looks when miserable.

entries.clue: Dicky and Fatty (4)

blocks.note: not a wobbly heart here: a pet form of Richard, and there is another short form
not a nickname: an adjective for heavy, creamy food

annotation.surface: Two nicknames, like a pair of comic sidekicks.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words read as schoolboy nicknames; Dicky and Rich are both short for Richard, and rich food is fatty.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a familiar short form of the name Richard, and food heavy with fat or cream.

entries.clue: Calling for the French? (6,1'4)

blocks.note: the surface wants shouting or phoning; in fact it is a vocation, a purpose in life
sounds like calling out to French people; it asks for the French phrase for that purpose

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether this is how the French call out or summon.
annotation.walkthrough: The French phrase means 'reason for being', the thing a person feels called to do.
annotation.definitionFit: A calling is a person's purpose in life, which is what this French phrase names in English usage.

entries.clue: Admitted what the sights may be (5,2)

blocks.note: not confessed: let in, as a lodger or a stray is
what a sightseer does to the view, absorbing it

annotation.surface: A tourist confessing how much of the scenery they managed to see.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Admitted' could mean confessed, but here it means let in; the second half is the tourist's idiom for looking around.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: received into a home or group, and absorbed by the eye, the idiom used of sightseeing.

entries.clue: Cores – or, reportedly, senior members of what sounds the same? (7)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: as reported in speech, so the sound is what counts

blocks.clueFragment: senior members of what sounds the same
blocks.note: colonels are senior officers of a corps, which sounds like 'cores'

annotation.surface: A puzzled query about the centres of fruit and whether some officers share their name.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue loops back on itself: 'what sounds the same' as cores is corps, whose senior members are colonels.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the soft inner seeds of nuts and fruit stones, and figuratively the central core of anything.

entries.clue: An idiot yesterday, in a manner of speaking (1,1,1,1)

annotation.definition: yesterday, in a manner of speaking

blocks.note: a fool, taken as two words: the article plus a short word for a gullible person

blocks.clueFragment: yesterday, in a manner of speaking
blocks.note: the office idiom 'I need it yesterday'

annotation.surface: Calling someone a fool for something they did yesterday.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration (1,1,1,1) signals an abbreviation; read as two words, the letters spell A SAP, a sap being a fool.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: demanding something 'yesterday' is a figure of speech for wanting it with the utmost urgency.

entries.clue: Southern facility by river restrained aquatic menace (3,7)

blocks.note: S = southern
doing something with facility is doing it with ease
R = river, as on maps
pent (up) = held in, restrained

annotation.surface: A creature kept in a riverside facility in the south of the country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Facility' looks like a building but means skill or ease.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the legendary long-bodied monster of sailors' tales, a menace in the water.

entries.clue: Present alternative rendering, albeit parallel – here represents a suitable example, primarily! (10)

indicatorNotes.primarily: take each word's primary, i.e. first, letter

blocks.clueFragment: Present alternative rendering, albeit parallel – here represents a suitable example
blocks.note: first letters of the ten words

annotation.surface: A teacher explaining how a paraphrase should run alongside the original.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter reuses the definition's three words to start the chain of initials, and the clue boasts it is itself a suitable example.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a verb: to restate a text in other words is to present an alternative rendering of it.

entries.clue: Those choosing prison for Spooner: might they be hampered? (10)

indicatorNotes.for Spooner: Rev. Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: nick = prison, so nick pickers; swap the initial sounds

annotation.surface: Wondering whether prisoners who chose jail would find themselves hindered.
annotation.walkthrough: In British slang the nick is prison. 'Hampered' looks like hindered, but a hamper is a lidded food basket.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun: people out for an alfresco meal typically carry a hamper, so they are 'hampered'.

entries.clue: Storage unit for socks, nip of putrid atmosphere (4)

indicatorNotes.nip of: a nip is a small bite, so just the first letter

blocks.note: first letter of putrid
air = atmosphere

annotation.surface: A sock drawer that smells bad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Storage unit' suggests a drawer, but it means the unit socks are sold, counted and put away in.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful definition: socks are counted and put away in twos, so the couple is their storage unit.

entries.clue: Used woolly thinking when lacking illumination? (7,5)

annotation.definition: Used woolly thinking when lacking illumination?

blocks.note: the surface wants muddled reasoning; in fact the thoughts are literally woolly, about fleecy animals
sounds like lacking insight; it means lying in the dark with the lights out

annotation.surface: Someone reasoning muddle-headedly for want of insight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Woolly thinking' is vague reasoning and 'illumination' reads as enlightenment; really someone is lying awake in the dark.
annotation.definitionFit: Tallying imaginary animals jumping a fence is the traditional remedy for sleeplessness after lights out.

entries.clue: Snack recipe concocted in experimental facilities (7,4)

indicatorNotes.concocted: cooked up, made by mixing ingredients

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: Food scientists devising a new snack in a laboratory.
annotation.walkthrough: The kitchen words 'recipe' and 'concocted' suit the surface and hide the mixing instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a campus of research laboratories and technology firms, where experimental work is housed.

entries.clue: Dinin’ on chocolate eggs, you say, in Steinbeck novel (4,2,4)

indicatorNotes.you say: spoken aloud, so the sound is what counts

blocks.note: chocolate eggs = Easter fare; dinin' on = feedin'

annotation.surface: A character in a Steinbeck novel gorging on chocolate eggs, written in dialect.
annotation.walkthrough: The dropped g in 'Dinin’' tells you to drop it in 'feedin'' too; said quickly, the two words run into the title.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: John Steinbeck's 1952 Salinas Valley family saga, later a James Dean film.

entries.clue: Film in Almodóvar’s language for the White House (10)

indicatorNotes.in Almodóvar’s language: Pedro Almodóvar is a Spanish director, so translate into Spanish

blocks.note: casa = house in Spanish
blanca = white in Spanish; Spanish puts the adjective after the noun

annotation.surface: A Spanish-language film made about the US presidential residence.
annotation.walkthrough: Spanish adjectives follow the noun, so the translation swaps the English order.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the 1942 wartime romance starring Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman.

entries.clue: Walk out on salsa band onstage for using a sample (7)

indicatorNotes.for using a sample: only a sample of the letters is used

blocks.note: salsA BAND ONstage

annotation.surface: A salsa band's gig ruined when it samples someone else's music and a performer storms off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sample' reads as a musical sample, apt for a band, but it signals a stretch of letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to desert someone, leaving them behind for good.

entries.clue: Evidently clumsy type – and a loafer (7)

blocks.note: one who keeps losing their footing, as the word itself shows
not an idler: a soft slip-on shoe

annotation.surface: Describing a clumsy, lazy person.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loafer' looks like an idler, but it is a shoe; 'Evidently' flags that the first sense is coined from slip.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: soft indoor footwear like a loafer, and jokingly someone who slips.

entries.clue: Swallowing duck, one checks for poison; I say ‘Cheers!’ (7)

annotation.definitionNote: the answer speaks: the toaster is the one who says it

indicatorNotes.Swallowing: what is swallowed ends up inside, so the taster's word takes the duck into its middle

blocks.note: a food taster tests a ruler's meal for poison
a duck is a zero score in cricket, shaped like O

annotation.surface: A royal food taster downs some duck and raises a glass.
annotation.walkthrough: T(O)ASTER. 'Duck' looks like the meal, but it is the letter O.
annotation.definitionFit: The answer speaks as someone proposing a toast, whose word is 'Cheers!'

entries.clue: Appreciate fizzy ale, Sire? (7)

indicatorNotes.fizzy: bubbling, so the letters are agitated

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A servant asking the king whether he enjoys sparkling beer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Appreciate' suggests enjoying the drink; it means understand.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of understanding: to become fully aware of something.

entries.clue: Residents x workers? (7)

blocks.note: X is the Roman numeral ten
worker ants

annotation.surface: A formula multiplying residents by workers.
annotation.walkthrough: The lower-case x looks like a times sign; it is the Roman numeral.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: people who occupy rented property live there, so they are its residents.

entries.clue: Newspaper exposé showing Archer and friend scratching bottom (4-3)

indicatorNotes.scratching bottom: to scratch is to strike out, and in a down entry the bottom is the last letter

blocks.note: William Tell, the legendary Swiss archer
ALLY loses its last letter

annotation.surface: A tabloid scoop about Jeffrey Archer and a pal caught scratching their backsides.
annotation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, a British novelist and politician, was a tabloid fixture, but the archer here is William Tell.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a revealing story or memoir that discloses everything, the stock-in-trade of tabloids.

entries.clue: Sinful American peels back – and out (6,6)

indicatorNotes.back: going back means heading the other way, so the word is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: fallen = sinful, as in a fallen woman
A = American
turned round to SLEEP

annotation.surface: A wicked American peels something and then leaves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out' at the end looks like a departure; it means unconscious.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: someone dead to the world is said to be out, or out cold.

entries.clue: Relative somewhat daunted (4)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: only some of the word is used

blocks.note: dAUNTed

annotation.surface: A family member who is a little intimidated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat daunted' reads as mildly nervous; it means part of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a parent's sister is one kind of relative.

entries.clue: Jealousy picked up from leading characters in Nouvelle Vague? (4)

indicatorNotes.leading characters in: the leading letters are the first ones of each word
indicatorNotes.picked up: heard, as a radio picks up a signal, so the sound is what counts

blocks.note: N and V, the initials, spoken as letter names

annotation.surface: Rival film-makers envious of the French New Wave.
annotation.walkthrough: The Nouvelle Vague was the French New Wave cinema; 'leading characters' sounds like its stars but means initials.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: resentful longing for what someone else has, the green-eyed monster.

entries.clue: I appreciate that German is curt, having unpleasant air (4)

indicatorNotes.curt: cut short, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: DANKE, German for thank you, loses its last letter

annotation.surface: Thanking a German who is brusque and has an unpleasant manner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Air' reads as a manner or bearing; it means the atmosphere of a place.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a cellar that is damp, cold and musty has stale, unpleasant air.

entries.clue: Can Guaraní get translated for C. American? (10)

indicatorNotes.get translated: translated means moved or changed, so rearrange

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: Asking whether Guaraní, a South American language, can be translated for a Central American.
annotation.walkthrough: Guaraní is an indigenous language of Paraguay, so 'translated' reads naturally; C. is Central.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a native of the country between Honduras and Costa Rica is one Central American.

entries.clue: It goes well with curry, whichever way you look at it (4)

indicators: whichever way you look at it

indicatorNotes.whichever way you look at it: read forwards or backwards, it is the same

blocks.note: the setter reuses the definition: the word reads the same both ways

annotation.surface: An enthusiastic endorsement of a curry accompaniment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Whichever way you look at it' sounds like emphasis but tells you the word is a palindrome.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the leavened Indian flatbread torn and used to scoop up curry.

entries.clue: ‘Hot location acceptable’ – tiny oriental feline (5,5)

blocks.note: hell is proverbially hot
OK = acceptable
itty, as in itty-bitty

annotation.surface: An estate agent's blurb for a sweltering flat, followed by a little eastern cat.
annotation.walkthrough: The word break falls inside the second piece, so the O of 'acceptable' ends the first word and its K starts the second.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Japanese Sanrio cartoon cat with a red bow is one feline from the Orient.
